text: Every time you write a for loop, Python is quietly using two functions: iter and next.
iter turns a list into an iterator — an object that knows how to hand out items one at a time.
Then next pulls the values in order, one call at a time, until they run out.
[chuckle] So a for loop is really just iter, then next over and over, catching the end automatically.
When the iterator is exhausted, next raises StopIteration, which is the loop's signal to stop.
[sniff] The powerful part is you can make your own iterables — any object with dunder iter and dunder next.
This Countdown class defines both, yielding numbers until it hits zero, then raising StopIteration.
So Python's own for loops and list function work on it, exactly like a built-in sequence.
[groan] Understanding iterators reveals what's really happening every time you loop over anything in Python.
